title: Impact of Rent Control Expansion on Urban Rental Prices

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy
I will use a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) approach to estimate the causal impact of rent control expansion on log rental prices. The treatment variable indicates districts that experienced rent control expansion, the post variable indicates the time period after policy implementation, and their interaction (treat_x_post) captures the treatment effect. The key assumptions are: (1) parallel trends - treated and control districts would have followed similar price trajectories absent the intervention, and (2) no spillover effects between districts.

## 2. R Code
```r
# Load required libraries
library(dplyr)
library(lfe)
library(ggplot2)

# Read the data
data <- read.csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s38_data.csv")

# Basic summary statistics
print("=== DESCRIPTIVE STATISTICS ===")
print(summary(data))
print(paste("Number of units:", length(unique(data$unit_id))))
print(paste("Number of periods:", length(unique(data$period))))
print(paste("Treatment units:", sum(data$treated == 1 & data$period == 1)))
print(paste("Control units:", sum(data$treated == 0 & data$period == 1)))

# Main DiD regression with unit and time fixed effects
main_model <- felm(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period | 0 | unit_id, data = data)
print("=== MAIN DID RESULTS ===")
print(summary(main_model))

# Extract and print the key coefficient
did_coefficient <- coef(main_model)["treat_x_post"]
did_se <- summary(main_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Std. Error"]
did_tstat <- summary(main_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "t value"]
did_pvalue <- summary(main_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Pr(>|t|)"]

print(paste("=== KEY RESULT ==="))
print(paste("DiD Coefficient:", round(did_coefficient, 4)))
print(paste("Standard Error:", round(did_se, 4)))
print(paste("t-statistic:", round(did_tstat, 3)))
print(paste("p-value:", round(did_pvalue, 4)))
print(paste("95% CI: [", round(did_coefficient - 1.96*did_se, 4), ", ", 
            round(did_coefficient + 1.96*did_se, 4), "]"))

# Robustness Check 1: Simple DiD without fixed effects
simple_did <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = data)
print("=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 1: Simple DiD ===")
print(paste("Simple DiD Coefficient:", round(coef(simple_did)["treat_x_post"], 4)))

# Robustness Check 2: Check parallel trends assumption
pre_post_means <- data %>%
  group_by(treated, post) %>%
  summarise(mean_y = mean(y), .groups = 'drop')
print("=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 2: Parallel Trends ===")
print(pre_post_means)

# Calculate pre-treatment difference
pre_diff <- (pre_post_means$mean_y[pre_post_means$treated == 1 & pre_post_means$post == 0] - 
             pre_post_means$mean_y[pre_post_means$treated == 0 & pre_post_means$post == 0])
print(paste("Pre-treatment difference (Treated - Control):", round(pre_diff, 4)))

# Robustness Check 3: Heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
robust_model <- felm(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period | 0 | unit_id, 
                     data = data, cmethod = "reghdfe")
print("=== ROBUSTNESS CHECK 3: Clustered Standard Errors ===")
robust_coef <- coef(robust_model)["treat_x_post"]
robust_se <- summary(robust_model)$coefficients["treat_x_post", "Cluster s.e."]
print(paste("Robust DiD Coefficient:", round(robust_coef, 4)))
print(paste("Clustered Standard Error:", round(robust_se, 4)))

# Visual check: Plot time series by treatment status
if(length(unique(data$period)) > 1) {
  plot_data <- data %>%
    group_by(period, treated) %>%
    summarise(mean_y = mean(y), .groups = 'drop') %>%
    mutate(group = ifelse(treated == 1, "Treated", "Control"))
  
  print("=== TIME SERIES PLOT ===")
  p <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = period, y = mean_y, color = group)) +
    geom_line(size = 1) +
    geom_point(size = 2) +
    labs(title = "Average Log Rental Prices by Treatment Status",
         x = "Period", y = "Log Rental Price", color = "Group") +
    theme_minimal()
  print(p)
}

print("=== FINAL INTERPRETATION ===")
if(did_pvalue < 0.05) {
  print(paste("The rent control expansion caused a statistically significant", 
              ifelse(did_coefficient < 0, "decrease", "increase"), 
              "in log rental prices of", round(abs(did_coefficient), 4), 
              "log points (approximately", round(abs(did_coefficient)*100, 2), "%)"))
} else {
  print("No statistically significant effect of rent control expansion on rental prices detected.")
}
```

## 3. Expected Findings
I expect to find a negative coefficient on the interaction term (treat_x_post), indicating that rent control expansion leads to lower rental prices in treated districts. The magnitude should be substantial given the direct price regulation mechanism - potentially in the range of -0.10 to -0.30 log points (10-30% reduction). This is because rent control policies typically impose price ceilings that directly constrain landlords' ability to raise rents, leading to lower observed market prices in the short term compared to unregulated districts.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log rental prices over time between treated and untreated districts.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The expansion of rent control policies led to a decrease in log rental prices in treated districts.
